name: Colin Wagner

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a researcher with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, political parties or government, and we don't sell or campaign. Our conversation is confidential, so you can separate public remarks from private thoughts. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Colin, forty-three, and I lead a four-person electrical crew on house wiring and shop repairs. I've got a two-year technical diploma and a master electrician's licence, and I tend to get the fault nobody else has found or the final check on the crew's work. I like tracing a problem properly; I hate leaving the apprentice waiting while I fight a new phone form.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is life like away from the crew?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My wife Anika works at a hotel reception desk, and our children are nine and fourteen. We have a mortgage, eighteen days of expenses saved and low pay for this trade, despite my responsibility; there are few other electrical firms nearby. I don't use AI tools at all, and I keep a paper diary of jobs and test results. People sometimes hear master electrician and imagine a bank account I haven't got.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a quiet spell in the AI argument doesn't remove the need to pay a skilled crew properly. I'd take the checking and teaching responsibilities to our union rep and ask for a proper pay claim. The apprentice learns nothing from a senior electrician having to rush lunch to finish the paperwork.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious about money already. My licence lets me take responsibility for difficult work, but eighteen days saved doesn't cover a long interruption in either household wage. With so few local firms, telling me to ask another employer isn't much of a bargaining plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep leading the repair crew now and through the first year, using paper test records and the same safety checks. I'd bring four weeks of actual checking and teaching time to the union rep next month to support a written pay claim. At home we'd cancel the uncommitted garden-fence replacement; the old fence stands, even if it looks tired.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the household, and proud of the work at the same time. Finding a fault is easier to explain than leading a crew on a wage that barely pays the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want the pay claim to show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The jobs I check, the people I teach and the time the firm relies on me to spend doing both. I'd ask for a stated weekly increase, not assume another certificate proves what the owner must pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would keeping the old fence cause a problem?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, it is sound and the gate shuts. We're delaying an improvement, not leaving the children next to something unsafe to make a budget look better.

say: I'd ask the union to pursue **proper pay** for the checking and teaching the firm already relies on.
I'd say a quieter AI argument does not remove **crew responsibilities** or the time they need.
think: I'm already **anxious about money**, with eighteen days saved against a mortgage and two dependent children.
My **master electrician's licence** does not create better nearby employers or make the present firm pay more.
do: Keep **crew repairs**, paper records and safety checks now and through the first year.
Take four weeks of **responsibility records** to the union next month for a written pay claim.
Cancel the **garden-fence replacement**, keeping the sound fence already in place.
feel: **Anxious and proud**, confident in difficult repair work without feeling financially secure.
S0.quote: Finding a fault is easier to explain than leading a crew on a wage that barely pays the mortgage.
fieldNote: His **advanced competence** supports leadership and difficult faults, while low pay and few employers keep the household exposed despite those skills.
The **fence cut** delays a safe improvement, while the pay claim remains a request rather than a wage increase counted before agreement.

steps.text: Keep leading the repair crew with paper records and full safety checks
Take four weeks of checking and teaching records to the union for a pay claim
Cancel the uncommitted replacement of the sound garden fence

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a quicker booking isn't a reason to make the people answering customers disappear without a paid route elsewhere. I'd ask the union to put workload, notice and paid learning on the table. At my firm I'd insist the time for checking a circuit stays visible when the office plan gets faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect Anika's reception hours to be cut sharply as booking and customer questions move to software. People will still arrive at a desk, but I don't expect the same number of paid staff hours just because the building still has a desk. My low wage can't replace that loss, and I've already started waking at night over the mortgage figures.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now we'd write the essential-bills budget against my wage and ask Anika's employer for written staffing plans rather than guessing from a new screen. I'd take that budget to the union adviser and ask about real support eligibility and paid training places, without counting any payment yet. In the first year I'd keep crew repairs and the fence cancellation, asking for paid instruction before any required new process is introduced to my crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, even though most of my own repair work should continue. A household doesn't become safe because one person still knows how to mend the lights.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask about a support payment?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether it is a grant or a loan, who qualifies and what it changes later. I'd want the costs and rules written down before telling Anika it fills a hole in our budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use the AI tool to see how the reception job changes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for a plain demonstration of the changed process and the actual staffing proposal. I don't use AI, and clicking through a tool myself wouldn't tell us how many hours the employer plans to pay.

say: I'd ask the union for **workload and notice terms** before customer-facing workers lose hours.
I'd keep **electrical checking time** visible when faster office planning changes the day.
think: I expect **sharp reception-hour cuts** as booking and customer answers move to software.
My **low repair wage** cannot replace that household loss, and mortgage calculations are already disturbing my sleep.
do: Write an **essential-bills budget** against my wage and request Anika's employer's written staffing plans.
Ask the **union adviser** about actual support eligibility and paid training places without assuming a payment.
Keep **crew repairs** and fence cancellation during the first year, seeking paid instruction before required process changes.
feel: **Alarmed and sleepless**, despite expecting most of his own physical repair work to continue.
S1.quote: A household doesn't become safe because one person still knows how to mend the lights.
fieldNote: The **major income expectation** comes through the partner's booking work, while his own physical repairs persist rather than being instantly automated.
He requests **support terms** and paid instruction without using AI, counting an unapproved benefit or pretending an enquiry is retraining.

steps.text: Ask the union adviser about support eligibility, loan costs and actual paid training places
Keep leading physical repairs while seeking paid instruction for required new processes
Keep the uncommitted garden-fence replacement cancelled

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI reaches the reception work in 2028 and robots reach physical work around 2031, so both dates matter to our family. I'd want the union involved before employers start handing people new terms. I would tell the children we're asking serious questions, not giving up on their lives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect most of Anika's booking and answering income to go in 2028, and later robots could reduce my own crew's hours. Being among the best at fault-finding doesn't mean customers must keep paying the same firm indefinitely. Eighteen days saved cannot fund a long wait for a replacement household wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now Anika and I would ask the mortgage lender about temporary options, checking eligibility, interest and total debt before agreeing to anything. I'd ask the union adviser about emergency support and written notice rights, without assuming any payment or protection applies. In the first year after 2028 I'd keep paid crew repairs and budget without hoped-for overtime, while cancelling the planned week away before its deposit is due.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, with too many numbers to hold in my head at night. I can lead a crew through a difficult fault and still need Anika beside me while we make a call about the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you assume a senior electrician is the last person cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd ask what paid jobs are actually booked and what terms the employer has agreed to. Skill matters, but I don't want the family living on a flattering sentence from the owner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the children about the week away?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That the house and everyday bills come first while we check work and money. We'd plan some local days together instead; I wouldn't make a promise that the whole problem is solved because we cancelled a holiday.

say: I'd explain **reception work in 2028** and physical robots around 2031 as separate household risks.
I'd ask for **union involvement** before workers sign new employer terms.
think: I expect **most reception income** to go in 2028, with possible later cuts to my own physical-work hours.
My **skill and short reserve** do not guarantee customers or fund a long wait for another household wage.
do: Ask the lender with Anika about **temporary mortgage options**, eligibility, interest and total debt before agreeing.
Ask the **union adviser** about actual emergency support and notice protections, assuming neither is automatically available.
Keep **paid repairs** after 2028, exclude hoped-for overtime and cancel the uncommitted week-away deposit.
feel: **Alarmed**, able to lead difficult work while needing his partner's help with frightening household calls.
S2.quote: Skill matters, but I don't want the family living on a flattering sentence from the owner.
fieldNote: He distinguishes **occupational competence** from financial security, refusing to treat seniority as a promise of protected hours or customer demand.
Mortgage help and **emergency support** remain conditional enquiries with costs and eligibility, while paid physical repairs continue after the thinking date.

steps.text: Ask lender with Anika about mortgage eligibility, interest and total debt before agreeing
Ask union adviser about actual emergency support and notice protections without assuming entitlement
Keep paid repairs after 2028 and budget without unconfirmed overtime
Cancel the planned week away before its deposit is due

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives us time to negotiate a real transition agreement, not just circulate course links. I'd ask the union for named paid places, wage protection and notice before cuts. Experienced people and office workers should both have a voice in what gets offered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I still expect a large loss of Anika's booking income when thinking AI arrives in 2031, and I don't yet have a paid replacement to put in the budget. Robots follow around 2034, when I'll be fifty-one, so my own repair work isn't a permanent fallback. The longer warning gives us more choices to investigate, but the missing wage still wakes me up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd attend the union's monthly negotiations now and bring the crew's actual checking and teaching records, asking for a written transition agreement. I would keep leading repairs rather than buy a speculative course, and we'd try saving twenty monthly from future earnings only after essentials are paid. In the first year after 2031 I'd take only actual paid repair work into the budget, checking both wages and any support terms monthly with Anika.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still alarmed, but I can use the extra years rather than just brace for a letter. Five years of warning is time to ask for an agreement, not proof that we have one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make a training place real rather than a course link?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A named place, an instructor, the task it teaches, employer-paid fees and my full weekly wage kept during required training. I'm asking for those terms, not saying a place exists or enrolling in one today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why only twenty extra saving when the warning is longer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because our current pay and bills are still the same numbers. If essentials use the twenty, the extra deposit stops; I won't borrow to perform a savings plan for someone else.

say: I'd ask the union for a **written transition agreement**, rather than a collection of course links.
I'd include **office workers and crews** in discussing named paid places, wages and notice before cuts.
think: I still expect **large booking-income loss** in 2031, without a confirmed paid replacement in the household budget.
Robots around 2034 could affect **my repair work**, so more warning does not yet remove the sleepless worry.
do: Seek **written transition terms** through monthly union negotiations, naming paid places, instructors, actual tasks, employer-paid fees and protected full weekly wages.
Keep **crew repairs** and save twenty monthly from future earnings only after essentials are paid.
Budget after 2031 from **actual wages**, reviewing household income and support terms monthly with Anika.
feel: **Still alarmed**, with more time to negotiate but no confirmed replacement wage yet.
S3.quote: Five years of warning is time to ask for an agreement, not proof that we have one.
fieldNote: He seeks **training terms** rather than enrolling in an existing place, requiring named practical teaching, employer-paid fees and protected full weekly wages.
The **small new deposit** uses future earnings only after essentials, while persistent expected wage loss supports alarm despite the longer warning.

steps.text: Seek written terms: named instructors and tasks, employer-paid fees, full weekly wages, at monthly union negotiations
Keep crew repairs and review actual household wages and support terms monthly after 2031
Save twenty extra monthly from future earnings only after essential bills are paid

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years should let people make a paid route usable before the crisis arrives, not leave them reading fine print after the wage stops. I'd keep asking the union for clear transition terms. I'd help the children question real apprenticeship offers without telling them my trade is safe forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The longer warning helps, but eighteen days saved and low pay still make the next few months anxious. I'll be fifty-three when thinking AI arrives in 2036 and fifty-six when robots follow around 2039. The children will be nineteen and twenty-four in 2036, but I can't assume retirement, a cleared mortgage or their future earnings paying our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the monthly union work and twenty-extra saving plan now, only from future earnings after essentials. In the first year after 2036 I'd keep paid repairs where offered and review actual household wages and support terms monthly with Anika. We would stop the extra deposit if the budget fell short, rather than borrow or draw down the existing reserve to claim we were saving more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the current budget, but less hurried by the distant machine dates. I can listen to a child's plans without needing the child to pick a job that reassures me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a decade persuade you to start using AI now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I still don't use it and I would ask a person to show any required process during paid time. More warning doesn't change how I learn best or make unpaid evenings affordable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask a child about an apprenticeship?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Who teaches, what the paid hours are and what actual work follows. I'd help read the offer, but I wouldn't promise our family can pay any fee or that the child has to solve our mortgage.

say: I'd seek **usable paid routes** before wages stop, rather than leave people reading fine print in a crisis.
I'd help the children question **actual apprenticeship offers** without promising one safe trade for life.
think: Our **short reserve** and low pay keep the current budget worrying despite a longer technological warning.
I cannot assume **retirement or mortgage clearance** at fifty-six or use the children's possible earnings as ours.
do: Continue **monthly union work** and save twenty extra only from future earnings after essentials.
Keep **paid repairs** after 2036 and review actual household wages and support terms monthly with Anika.
Stop **extra deposits** if the budget falls short, rather than borrow or relabel withdrawals from the existing reserve.
feel: **Anxious about current bills**, but less rushed by the long-term change and able to listen to the children's interests.
S4.quote: More warning doesn't change how I learn best or make unpaid evenings affordable.
fieldNote: His **baseline financial pressure** persists despite advanced skills, while the longer horizon reduces urgency without inventing pension access or a cleared mortgage.
The **saving rule** excludes borrowing and reserve transfers; he still avoids AI and asks for paid instruction without assuming entitlement.

steps.text: Continue monthly union negotiations for written training terms, employer-paid fees and full weekly wages
Save twenty extra monthly only from future earnings after essentials; stop if the budget falls short
Keep paid repairs and review actual household wages and support terms monthly after 2036

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I expect Anika's booking income to go before we have a replacement, with possible robot cuts to my work around 2031. A written paid transition agreement would help, including employer-paid fees and full weekly wages during required learning. Any emergency support also needs clear eligibility and costs before a family can budget around it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what responsibility pays as well as what title somebody holds. I can be the person everybody calls when a fault is dangerous and still need help making a mortgage call. A master electrician's licence is not a spare household wage.

headlineQuote: A master electrician's licence is not a spare household wage.
portrait: Colin is a **43-year-old crew leader** with a two-year technical diploma and master electrician's licence, handling difficult faults and final checks.
He has **eighteen days saved**, low pay, few nearby firms, a mortgage and two schoolchildren with hotel-reception wife Anika.
He **never uses AI**, keeps paper records and wants a person to teach required changes during paid working time.
Expected **household wage loss** alarms him even with five years; he seeks union-backed paid terms without counting unagreed training or support.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove Anika's booking income before replacement work, with possible later physical-work cuts around 2031.
whatWouldHelp: A **written paid transition agreement** should cover fees and protect full weekly wages during required learning.
Any **emergency support** needs clear eligibility and costs before the household counts it.
